area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can fly and explain a go-around from the right seat at VX or VY ±5 knots, teach a learner to decide early and to fly power, attitude and configuration against strong trim forces, and spot and fix the go-around errors learners make most.
why: The go-around is not dangerous in itself; it becomes dangerous only when it is delayed or flown badly, and the most critical one starts close to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Every learner you solo must first be trained in go-arounds [[60:272|14 CFR 61.87(d)(15)]], and the AFH puts the job of making it feel normal squarely on the flight instructor, who should stress early on that any approach may end in a go-around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

prereading.what: Go-arounds: reasons, landing expectancy and pride, power, attitude, configuration, ground effect and the common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 9-10 to 9-12

prereading.what: The stabilized approach criteria and the 500, 1,000 and 300 foot go-around gates.
prereading.label: AFH 9-6

prereading.what: Cross-control stall and the elevator trim stall demonstration, the instructor's tool for teaching go-around trim forces.
prereading.label: AFH 5-20 to 5-21

prereading.what: Flaps, trim and the pitch-up in a go-around; why consistent flap use gives a preplanned go-around.
prereading.label: AFH 12-4 to 12-5

prereading.what: Using distractions in training, habit patterns, letting learners correct their own errors, and solo radio discipline.
prereading.label: AIH 9-10 to 9-12

prereading.what: LAHSO responsibilities, rejected landing after LAHSO, and the low approach.
prereading.label: AIM 4-3-11 to 4-3-12

prereading.what: Overrun hazards that should trigger a go-around: unstabilized approach, excess speed, height over the threshold, long touchdown, tailwind.
prereading.label: AC 91-79B 5-1 to 5-3

warmup: Think first: your pre-solo learner has never once gone around on their own. Every time an approach went bad, you said 'go around' and they did it well. Today the approach is fast and high at 200 feet and they keep going, glancing at you. Is the problem their hands, their judgment, or something you taught them without meaning to? What will you change on the next circuit?

key_terms.def: A normal maneuver used when approach and landing parameters deviate from expectations or continuing is hazardous [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].
The three go-around priorities, in order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
The belief that conditions are less threatening than they are and the approach is sure to end in a safe landing; one of the two usual sources of go-around delay [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

A final approach on a constant path with airspeed, configuration, descent rate and power in set limits; in the pattern, go around at once if it becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
The throttle, which adds or removes total energy; the elevator only distributes energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].
A first trim adjustment after the go-around airspeed and climb pitch are set, to relieve heavy control pressures; finer trim comes once conditions settle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
A demonstration of the stall that can follow full power with nose-up landing trim set, when the pilot does not keep positive control [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Reduced induced drag near the surface. In a go-around it is borrowed performance that is repaid on climbing out [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Land and hold short operations: landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, taxiway or other designated point [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]].

Any occurrence in the runway environment involving an aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard or loss of separation with an aircraft taking off or landing [[1:365|PHAK 14-31]].
A false feeling of nose-up pitch from rapid acceleration, worst with poor visual references; the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].
A go-around after an approach without touching the runway; made straight ahead with no turns or climb until a visual check for traffic, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]].

chunks.title: The go-around and the standard you hold

body.p: A go-around is a normal maneuver. The AFH lists reasons to discontinue an approach: ATC requirements, a hazard that appears on the runway, overtaking another airplane, wind shear, wake turbulence, a mechanical failure, or an unstable approach [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Like any normal maneuver it should be practiced and perfected [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

The procedure rests on three cardinal principles, in order: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, flaps come up (at least partly) before the gear, and the gear comes up after a positive rate of climb [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Item
Private ACS (your learner)
Flight Instructor ACS (you)
rows: Power and climb pitch
VX or VY as appropriate, +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.N.S4)
VX or VY as appropriate, ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.N.S4)
Climb to a safe maneuvering altitude
VY +10/-5 knots (ACS PA.IV.N.S7)
VY ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.N.S7)
How it is flown
Flown
Demonstrated while you simultaneously explain (ACS AI.VII.N Skills)

body.p: Your two exact standards read: “Apply takeoff power immediately and transition to climb pitch attitude for VX or VY as appropriate ±5 knots” (ACS AI.VII.N.S4) and “Maintain VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude” (ACS AI.VII.N.S7).

callout.text: Power, attitude, configuration. The order is the lesson: the airplane needs energy first, a safe pitch second, and less drag only after the descent has stopped [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Your trainer's VY is 79 KIAS. What climb window does the examiner hold you to after a go-around, and what window applies to your private learner?
check.a: You: 74 to 84 KIAS (VY ±5, ACS AI.VII.N.S7). Learner: 74 to 89 KIAS (VY +10/-5, ACS PA.IV.N.S7).

chunks.title: Stabilized approach and energy: where the decision comes from

body.p: The go-around decision is easiest when the learner has a clear picture of 'normal.' The AFH gives these criteria for a typical piston airplane, and asks pilots to focus on what leads to a stable approach rather than insisting on every item [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

head: Criterion
Stabilized when [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
rows: Glide path
Typically a constant 3 degrees to the touchdown zone, obstructions permitting
Heading
Tracking the centerline with only minor corrections; bank normally 15 degrees or less on final
Airspeed
Within +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed (AFM, 1.3 VSO, or placard)
Configuration
Landing configuration, gear down, in trim
Descent rate
Generally 500 to 1,000 fpm; if more than 500 fpm, reduce it before 300 feet AGL
Power
Appropriate to the configuration and not below the AFM minimum for approach
Briefings and checklists
Done before the approach, except the landing checklist

body.p: The gates: go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC or 1,000 feet in IMC. In a typical GA piston traffic pattern, go around immediately if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Energy: the throttle is the total energy controller and the elevator distributes that energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. When altitude and speed are off in the same direction it is a total energy error for the throttle; when they are off in opposite directions it is a distribution error for the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Application: a go-around is the largest total-energy correction there is, and the elevator then decides whether that energy goes into speed or climb.

Very slow is a different animal. Full throttle may give no surplus at all, and then the only recourse is to push forward first to cut angle of attack and drag, then add energy; near the ground there may not be room [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. The airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

The overrun view: AC 91-79B lists unstabilized approaches, excess speed (about 20% more distance for 10% more speed), excess height (about 200 feet more distance for each 10 feet above 50) and landing past the touchdown point the POH assumed, after which the calculated distance may not be achievable [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]] [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]]. It is the pilot's responsibility to tell ATC when an instruction will cause an unstabilized approach because of speed or descent rate [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].

callout.text: A low learner may grab the flaps to 'stretch' the approach. Retracting flaps to fix an undershoot can cause a sudden loss of lift, an excessive sink rate and a worse unstable approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. If the approach is very high or very low, the normal answer is a go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

check.q: Field elevation 820 feet, VMC. Passing 1,320 feet MSL your learner is still adding flaps and is 15 knots fast. What do the AFH gates say?
check.a: 1,320 feet MSL is the 500-foot gate. Not stabilized there, so go around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

chunks.title: Why pilots wait: expectancy, pride and indecision

body.p: A go-around can be needed anywhere in the landing, but the most critical one starts very close to the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Delay usually has two sources, and indecision and delay are both on the AFH list of common errors [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Source of delay
What it is
How you teach against it
rows: Landing expectancy (set)
Belief that conditions are less threatening than they are and the approach will surely end safely [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Treat every approach as one that may end in a missed approach or go-around [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]; brief the decision points before final
Pride
Belief that going around admits failure to fly the approach properly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Stress from the start that any approach may end in a go-around and that 'poor approach equals poor pilot' is a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Indecision
Hesitating when prompt action is required; deciding not to decide is a wrong decision [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]
Practice the call at a set gate until it is automatic; 'When in doubt, go around' [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]

body.p: Pride often sounds like the macho attitude, 'I can do it,' whose antidote is 'Taking chances is foolish' [[30:20|RMH 3-2]] [[30:21|RMH 3-3]]. Landing expectancy sounds like invulnerability, 'It won't happen to me' [[30:20|RMH 3-2]]. Application: name the attitude in the debrief, kindly, so the learner can hear it in their own head next time.

Plan continuation: AC 91-79B warns that plan continuation bias can drive actions counter to established rules, and recommends briefing contingencies during low workload so that in the terminal area the pilot executes the briefed plan instead of analyzing risk [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.1]] [[27:20|AC 91-79B 3.12.2]]. For a learner, the briefed plan is the gate list from the last chunk.

callout.text: When there is doubt about the outcome of an approach, go around, evaluate, and decide whether to try again or divert [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]. Teach the learner that doubt itself is the trigger; they do not need proof that the landing will fail.

check.q: On short final your learner is floating with airspeed bleeding off and says, 'It always settles in eventually.' Which source of delay is this, and what is your one-word call?
check.a: Landing expectancy, the belief that the approach is sure to end safely [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The call is 'Go around' [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

chunks.title: Power: all of it, smoothly, right now

body.p: Power is the first concern. The instant the decision is made, apply full or maximum allowable takeoff power smoothly and without hesitation, and hold it until flying speed and controllability are restored. A settling airplane has inertia, and it takes power to stop the descent [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

bullets: Smooth but positive: abrupt throttle movement makes some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. 'Abrupt power application' is a listed error, and so is 'failure to apply maximum allowable power in a timely manner' [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Carburetor heat goes off to get maximum power, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Constant-speed propeller: for maximum takeoff power the propeller control goes full forward (low pitch, high rpm) and the throttle to maximum allowable manifold pressure [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

Mixture at a high-elevation airport: a full-rich mixture gets progressively richer as air density drops, which can cause roughness and an appreciable loss of power [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. What setting to carry on final there is a POH/AFM question.

body.p: Why it matters for teaching: the power step is where a learner's hesitation shows. A hand that stops halfway, then waits, is indecision you can see. Application: watch the throttle hand, not just the airspeed, and debrief what you saw.

callout.text: Power alone does not fix low and slow. If the airplane is very slow, full throttle may not create surplus energy, and the nose may need to come down first [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. Do not let a learner add power and pull at the same time from a mushing approach.

check.q: Why does carburetor heat come off during the power step?
check.a: To obtain maximum power, as applicable [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

body.p: The pilot must accept that the airplane cannot fly below stall speed and cannot climb below minimum power required speed, and resist any urge to pitch up when airspeed is short. Sometimes it is right to lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

At the moment of the decision the airplane is trimmed for low airspeed. Sudden power raises the nose and yaws the airplane left. Letting the nose rise too early can cause an unrecoverable stall when the go-around is low, so expect considerable forward elevator pressure and enough right rudder for torque and P-factor. Once airspeed and climb pitch are set, rough trim; trim finely when things settle [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Flaps add to the pitch story. Trim was set to offset the flaps' nose-down pitching moment, and full power increases airflow over the wing, so pitch changes a lot. The pitch-up does not go away completely with flap retraction because of the trim setting, so be ready for rapid changes in pitch forces [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

If the go-around starts from low airspeed, such as from the round out, a bad bounce or an inadvertent approach to a stall, temper the pitch-up: control and flying speed come first, and a few moments of level or near-level flight may be needed while the airplane accelerates [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

Teach the trim force at altitude first with the elevator trim stall demonstration: configure, trim nose-up for the glide, then advance to maximum power as for a go-around. Propwash and trim make the nose rise sharply and turn left; before a stall, apply forward pressure to cut the angle of attack and kill the stall warning, return to a normal climb attitude, then trim [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. It is a demonstration-only maneuver that only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform on a practical test [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

VX or VY: VX gives the most height over a distance, VY the most height in the least time [[24:142|AFH 6-10]]. Choose VX only if something must be cleared, then VY. Expect a lower climb pitch when heavy or when density altitude limits power [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

callout.text: Patter for your demo: 'Full power, carb heat off. Feel the nose come up: forward pressure, right rudder, hold this picture. Rough trim.' The AFH order of power, then attitude with rudder and rough trim, gives you the script [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner adds full power from a nose-up trimmed, full-flap glide and lets the nose come up on its own. What happens, and what should their hands do?
check.a: Propwash and trim pitch the nose sharply up and left, above climb attitude, toward a stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Forward pressure and right rudder hold a safe attitude, then rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Configuration: flaps in steps, then gear, then the checklist

body.p: With climb attitude and power set, flap retraction comes next. After the descent has stopped, the landing flaps go partly up or to the takeoff setting the manufacturer recommends. Depending on height and airspeed, retract in small steps so the airplane can accelerate as they come up. A sudden, complete retraction can cause a loss of lift and settle the airplane into the ground [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, flaps come up (at least partly) before the gear for two reasons: full flaps make more drag than the gear on most airplanes, and if the airplane touches down as the go-around starts, you want the gear down and locked. The gear comes up after a positive rate of climb, after rough trim, and when it is certain the airplane will stay airborne [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

Consistency pays off here. Extending the same flaps at the same point in the pattern on every landing gives a preplanned, familiar go-around sequence for each position in the pattern [[24:236|AFH 12-5]]. During the go-around, monitor pitch and airspeed, control flap retraction to minimize altitude loss and use rudder for coordination [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

The opposite risk is a high-drag go-around where the pilot forgets to raise gear or flaps; it is one of the AFH's examples of draining energy at low altitude toward an irreversible sink [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

Checklists: review the POH balked-landing checklist as workload permits, and if you return to land, redo the entire before-landing checklist. A go-around interrupts habit patterns and is a classic setup for a gear-up landing [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. Some airplanes have a gear retraction speed well below the extension speed, so watch it during the cleanup [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

callout.text: In airplanes with high control pressures at maximum power, reaching for the flap handle can be the moment control is lost. Airplane control is the first consideration in this high-workload phase [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Also watch which handle the learner grabs: positively identify gear and flap controls before moving them [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

check.q: At 80 feet your learner moves the flap lever from full to zero in one motion. What will you see, and what is the fix?
check.a: A loss of lift and the airplane settling toward the ground. Retract in small increments as the airplane accelerates, after the descent has stopped [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

chunks.title: Ground effect and the very low go-around

body.p: Ground effect is a factor in every takeoff and landing and can be one in a go-around. The 'cushion of air' that seems to help the change from descent to climb is imaginary: it is reduced induced drag, borrowed performance that is repaid on climbing out. A premature climb may leave the airplane unable to climb, or even hold altitude, at full power [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Ground effect fades quickly with height and is negligible at about one wingspan. Climbing out of it takes more angle of attack, and induced drag rises [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

In an extremely low go-around the airplane may settle onto the runway and bounce. That is not particularly dangerous if it is kept straight at a constant, safe pitch; the power soon gives flying speed and cushions any second touchdown [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The initial part of a go-around is slow-speed flight, near stall or the region of reversed command [[23:85|IFH 4-8]].

callout.text: 'Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely' is a listed go-around error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Coach a pause: 'Hold it level, let it accelerate.'

check.q: Why can a go-around started a few feet over the runway feel strong and then sag as the airplane climbs?
check.a: Near the ground induced drag is reduced; that borrowed performance is repaid when the airplane leaves ground effect [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:142|AFH 6-10]].

body.p: Thin air reduces engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. More weight, more altitude, gear down and flaps down all reduce excess power, so climb performance falls with each [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Application: a go-around starts with gear and flaps down, often heavy and slow, so on a hot day at a high field every one of these stacks against you.

The climb pitch will be lower when the airplane is heavy or power is limited by density altitude [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]. Under high density altitude, high temperature or maximum weight, an airplane may fly in ground effect yet be unable to climb out of it [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

Landing speed is set at a minimum safe speed that leaves margin above the stall and gives satisfactory control and capability for a go-around [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]]. A learner who drags the approach slow is spending the go-around margin.

head: Condition
Effect on the go-around decision or climb
Source
rows: Wind (gusts and turbulence)
Fly a power-on approach slightly above normal speed; a common practice adds half the gust factor; partial flaps help control in a gusty crosswind
Wind (crosswind near the ground)
It can change markedly within a few hundred feet, so check the ground track often in the climb
Wind (tailwind on landing)
About 21% more landing distance for the first 10 knots, which makes a long touchdown a go-around trigger sooner
Increasing headwind shear
Airspeed rises and the nose tends to pitch up; near convective weather a large gain may come before a loss and is a reason to discontinue the approach
Increasing tailwind shear
Airspeed and performance drop and the nose tends to pitch down
Density altitude
Less power, thrust and lift; lower climb pitch and weaker climb

callout.text: Before a lesson at a hot or high field, brief the learner that the go-around climb picture will be lower and the climb slower, so a weak climb does not surprise them into pulling the nose up.

check.q: Name the three things thin air takes away, and what it does to the go-around climb pitch.
check.a: Engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. The climb pitch will be lower when density altitude limits power [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].

chunks.title: Wind correction: from wing-low final to crabbed climb

body.p: On a crosswind final there are two methods, crab and wing-low. Wing-low is recommended in most cases, a mix may be used, and pilots should learn both [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. In wing-low, rudder aligns the nose with the runway and aileron sets just enough bank to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

A crosswind go-around changes from landing technique to departure technique. As the airplane establishes its climb, turn the nose into the wind, level the wings and adjust rudder to crab along the extended centerline. The crosswind can change markedly within a few hundred feet of the ground, so check the ground track often and adjust the wind correction angle [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

Flaps make crosswind control harder. With flaps out, the upwind wing is more affected, and lateral control gets harder as flaps near full and the wind nears 90 degrees [[24:235|AFH 12-4]]. Application: retracting flaps in steps during the go-around also gives back lateral control.

bullets: What you watch for: the learner keeps the sideslip deep into the climb, so the airplane stays cross-controlled and slow to climb.
Or the learner levels the wings at full power and forgets the crab, and the climb drifts downwind toward parallel traffic.
Fix: one prompt, 'Turn into the wind, wings level, track the centerline,' then make them name the ground reference they are tracking [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

callout.text: Land in a sideslip, climb in a crab. Low and slow over the runway: wing-low. Climbing away: nose into the wind, wings level [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

check.q: Your learner goes around from a wing-low final in a right crosswind. Once climbing, how should the airplane look?
check.a: Nose turned right into the wind, wings level, rudder adjusted so the track stays over the extended centerline [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

chunks.title: Traffic: the side-step, radio calls and the pattern

body.p: Collision hazards drive many go-arounds. If the turn to final would create a collision hazard, a go-around or avoidance maneuver is in order, and rushing the turn to make room behind another airplane is a good reason to abandon the approach. If traffic on the runway may not clear in time, an early go-around may be in order; a pilot may go around and inform the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

If the go-around is due to conflicting traffic on the ground or in the air, consider maneuvering to the side to keep it in sight, which may mean a slight turn to offset from the runway [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. The upwind leg, parallel to the runway, is flown after go-arounds, and once at a safe altitude a shallow turn to the upwind side gives a better view of departing aircraft [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

bullets: Nontowered: after a takeoff or go-around, continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway, staying aware of traffic in the pattern [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]] [[1:355|PHAK 14-21]]. If staying in the pattern, turn crosswind only beyond the departure end and within 300 feet of pattern altitude [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].
Radio, nontowered: communicate your position to avoid a traffic conflict; following the standard pattern also avoids excessive maneuvering down low [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Radio, towered: when told 'go around' with no other instructions, a VFR airplane overflies the runway climbing to pattern altitude and enters the pattern via the crosswind leg [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]. For a planned low approach in a Class B, C or D surface area, ask the tower before starting final [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]].

Wake: departing behind a larger aircraft, climb above its path until turning clear and avoid headings that cross below and behind it; after a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, allow at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: How to teach the side-step: keep it small, coordinated and only as much as needed to see the traffic. Application: a learner who 'side-steps' with a steep, skidding turn at 100 feet has traded one hazard for a worse one, which leads straight into the low-altitude chunk.

check.q: Nontowered field, pattern altitude 1,000 feet AGL. After a go-around, what is the earliest point you may start the crosswind turn?
check.a: Beyond the departure end of the runway and within 300 feet of pattern altitude, so at or above 700 feet AGL [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]].

body.p: LAHSO: the pilot in command has final authority to accept or decline, and should decline if it compromises safety. Student pilots or pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not participate. Available Landing Distance (ALD) is published in the Chart Supplement and Terminal Procedures Publications [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. Pilots should only receive a LAHSO clearance with at least a 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

An accepted LAHSO clearance must be followed like any clearance unless amended or in an emergency, but it does not preclude a rejected landing. If a rejected landing becomes necessary, maintain safe separation from other aircraft or vehicles and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

Application, what to teach: a rejected LAHSO landing climbs over or near the intersection where the crossing runway's traffic was the reason for the hold-short. Brief it before accepting: where the conflicting traffic will be, which way you will offset to keep it in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]], and the words you will say to the tower.

Runway incursions: about 65% are caused by pilots, and almost half of those by GA pilots [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. The three main causal areas are failure to comply with ATC instructions, lack of airport familiarity and nonconformance with standard operating procedures [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]]. Landing without clearance is a pilot deviation that can become an incursion [[1:366|PHAK 14-32]].

bullets: Someone else's incursion: an aircraft or vehicle on your runway is a listed reason to go around [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Decide early and inform the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Your own: on final verify the runway number and alignment; if there is any doubt about the landing surface, go around and sort it out [[24:175|AFH 9-4]].
Your own, LAHSO: if you land, exit before the hold-short point or stop at it [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. A go-around is better than a late, uncertain stop.

callout.text: Controllers need a full readback of every LAHSO clearance including the words 'hold short of' the runway, taxiway or point [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: Towered field, 200 feet on final: a fuel truck crosses the hold line onto your runway and the tower says nothing. What two things does the AFH say you may do?
check.a: Go around, early, and inform the controller [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin, CFIT, distraction and disorientation

body.p: Stall and spin: a skidding cross-control stall most often comes from an overshot base-to-final turn fixed with more bank, back pressure and bottom rudder. The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around, without bank over 30 degrees or a skidding turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The AFH's examples of draining energy at low altitude include slow approaches, high-drag go-arounds and steep pattern turns [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

CFIT: causes include flight at night, high density altitude and intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. A go-around at night or at a high, hot field brings all three close. Following established pattern procedures removes excessive maneuvering at low altitude [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

Disorientation: rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff, can create the somatogravic illusion of a nose-up attitude, especially with poor visual references, and the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Application: a full-power go-around over a dark area at night is the same acceleration. Teach a deliberate look at the attitude indicator; habits of instrument cross-check built early give better airspeed control and landings [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Distractions and priorities: the instructor teaches the learner to divide attention between a distracting task and aircraft control, and to take charge, even telling a passenger or an examiner when their actions interfere [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]. In the go-around, airplane control is the first consideration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Situational awareness means knowing aircraft position, flight path, other aircraft, the environment and the human factors in play, and planning what comes next [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

callout.text: Your own risk as the instructor: too much talking near the ground can cost collision avoidance and situational awareness, and can drown out radio calls. Use only concise prompting on approaches [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. If the learner freezes or the go-around turns unsafe, take control without hesitation [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner overshoots the turn to final at 400 feet and starts feeding in bottom rudder to 'bring the nose around.' What is the safest action, and why?
check.a: Go around. Bottom rudder with more bank and back pressure sets up a skidding cross-control stall that can spin, and the AFH names the go-around as the safest answer to an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Start the framing on day one: the instructor should emphasize early that any approach or landing may end in a go-around, and that blaming a go-around on poor skill is a fallacy [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. The law of effect says behavior followed by a satisfying outcome tends to repeat, so make a timely go-around feel like the success it is [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

head: Stage
What you do
What you say or ask
rows: Ground brief
Walk power, attitude, configuration and the decision gates for your airplane [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
'A go-around is a normal maneuver. Whoever says it first, we do it, no debate.'
At altitude
Demonstrate the elevator trim stall, then go-arounds from a simulated final, so trim forces are felt with height to spare [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
'Feel how hard the nose wants to come up? That push is the lesson.'
Pattern, instructor-called
Call go-arounds at varied heights, including low ones in ground effect [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Use the concrete words 'Go around', not 'do something' [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]
Pattern, learner-called
Let a mildly bad approach develop, safety permitting, and see if the learner calls it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Debrief: 'What told you, and when?'
Vary it
Combine it with crosswinds, traffic or a different flap setting to test understanding [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
'Same go-around, flaps 20 this time. What changes?'
Before solo
Confirm the learner goes around without being prompted [[60:272|14 CFR 61.87(d)(15)]]
Agree you will not talk to them on short final during the solo [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

body.p: Use real moments. A deer crossing the runway on final is the AIH's own example of a teachable moment to stress always being ready to go around [[25:63|AIH 3-12]]. AC 91-79B asks instructors to stress decision-making and include runway overrun mitigation in training, and names the go-around and its reasons as part of a training program [[27:38|AC 91-79B 5.3.2]] [[27:38|AC 91-79B 5.3.3]].

Analyze and correct: the AFH's ten common errors are your checklist for what to watch [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Safety permitting, let a learner go partway into an error and find the way out, since learners rarely learn a maneuver well without chances to correct it [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Near the ground there is less room, so decide before the flight how far you will let each error go.

callout.text: Risks of teaching it: a learner who freezes with full power and nose-up trim, a learner who grabs all the flaps at once, and your own late call. Be ready to take control at any time on a learner's first attempts at a hazardous maneuver [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner always goes around well when you call it, but never calls it on their own. What change in your lesson plan addresses that?
check.a: Add learner-called go-arounds: let a mildly poor approach develop, safety permitting, so the learner must recognize it and decide [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], then debrief what cue they used. Recognition failure is the first listed error [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

body.p: These are the AFH's ten common go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The 'what you see' and 'fix' columns come from the AFH go-around procedure unless another source is named.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to recognize a condition that warrants a rejected landing
Continuing past a gate, fast and high, or past a runway hazard
Teach the stabilized criteria and gates [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; ask 'What is our gate?' on each final
Indecision
Partial power in and out, eyes going to you for permission
Teach that not deciding is a wrong decision [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]; 'when in doubt, go around' [[24:193|AFH 9-22]]
Delay in initiating a go-around
The decision comes, but only very close to the ground
Name expectancy or pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; praise early calls
Failure to apply maximum allowable power in a timely manner
Throttle short of the stop, slow acceleration, carb heat left on
Full power the instant the decision is made, carb heat off [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Abrupt power application
Throttle slammed forward, engine stumbles in some airplanes
Smooth but positive throttle movement [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Improper pitch attitude
Nose rising above the climb picture with the stall horn, or a dive to gain speed near the ground
Forward pressure against trim, hold a safe climb attitude, rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Failure to configure the airplane appropriately
All flaps up at once and the airplane settles, or full flaps still down well into the climb
Flaps in small steps after the descent stops; gear after a positive rate [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely
A strong start, then no climb or a sink at full power
Hold a level or near-level attitude while the airplane accelerates [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]
Failure to adequately compensate for torque/P factor
Nose yawing left and the ball out as power comes in
Right rudder as the power comes in [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]
Loss of aircraft control
Reaching for flaps while the nose climbs; drift off the extended centerline
Control first, then configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; crab along the centerline [[24:140|AFH 6-8]]

body.p: On the checkride the examiner often flies a simulated error as your 'learner.' Say three things in order: what you saw, the likely cause, and the fix, then have the learner fly it again.

callout.text: Many of these errors share a root: a learner who has only flown go-arounds when told to. Mix instructor-called and learner-called go-arounds in every pattern lesson.

check.q: The airplane climbs nicely to 15 feet after power is added, then stops climbing with full power and the airspeed stuck low. Which listed error is this?
check.a: Attempting to climb out of ground effect prematurely [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-12. Go-around procedure. (AFH 9-11)
f1.alt: An airplane descends toward a runway, then levels off low with the labels Timely decision to make go-around and Apply max power, adjust pitch attitude, and allow airspeed to increase. It then climbs: Assume climb attitude, flaps to intermediate; Positive rate of climb, retract gear, climb at VY; Retract remaining flaps; and 500 feet cruise climb.

f2.caption: Figure 4-12. The control skills needed to correct total energy and energy distribution errors. (AFH 4-13)
f2.alt: A grid with altitude rows Higher, Desired altitude and Lower, and airspeed columns Cautions when Very Slow, Slower, Desired speed and Faster. Each box gives the throttle and elevator correction. Box 5 in the center is the desired energy state. The very slow and lower box is red and marked Dangerous: apply full throttle and avoid pitching up on the backside of the power required curve.

f3.caption: Figure 5-14. Elevator trim stall. (AFH 5-21)
f3.alt: Airplane sequence: configured for landing and trimmed nose-up; maximum power applied for a simulated go-around lets the nose rise; before a full stall the pilot applies forward pressure, eliminates the stall warning and re-trims; return to the desired flightpath.

f4.caption: Figure 12-5. Flaps extended pitching moment. (AFH 12-5)
f4.alt: Two wing sections. Top: flap slightly deflected, center of pressure and lift arrow behind the center of gravity, a small pitching moment and a small tail down force. Bottom: flap deflected much more, the lift arrow moves farther aft, the pitching moment circle is larger and the tail down force arrow is much larger.

f5.caption: Figure 6-6. Crosswind climb flightpath. (AFH 6-9)
f5.alt: Top view of the departure end of a runway (the far end is marked 18) with wind blowing from the left. An airplane is shown four times along the centerline: rolling straight, lifting off, then turning its nose into the wind, and finally crabbed with its nose into the wind while its track stays over the extended centerline.

f6.caption: Figure 14-39. Traffic pattern operations, single runway. (PHAK 14-22)
f6.alt: A standard left-hand traffic pattern around a single runway on a green background. Numbered red dots mark points along the pattern: 1 on the 45-degree entry to downwind, 2 on downwind, 3 at the turn to final, 4 just past the departure end of the runway on the departure leg, 5 on the crosswind leg, and two dots marked 6 on the straight-out and 45-degree departure paths. A segmented circle with a wind cone sits beside the runway.

scenario.title: Hot, high and busy: a pre-solo go-around lesson
scenario.setup: Your pre-solo learner flies a fixed-gear, carbureted trainer with 40 degrees of flaps at a nontowered airport, elevation 5,200 feet, on a 92 °F afternoon. Wind 240 at 10 gusting 18, landing runway 26. A Bonanza is taxiing toward the runway 26 hold line, and a Cessna is two miles behind you on final. The learner is tired after a long lesson and wants 'just one more landing.'

questions.q: Before this circuit, what do you brief about how the go-around will feel here compared with your sea-level home field?
questions.a: Thin air cuts power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]], and gear and flaps down cut excess power further [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Expect a lower climb pitch [[24:137|AFH 6-5]] and a weak climb, and do not try to climb out of ground effect too soon [[24:143|AFH 6-11]].

questions.q: On a gusty final the learner flies normal approach speed with full flaps. What do you suggest, and why does it matter for a go-around?
questions.a: A common practice is normal speed plus half the gust factor, here about 4 knots, with partial flaps for control in a gusty crosswind, within POH guidance [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. Landing speed is meant to leave capability for a go-around [[1:272|PHAK 11-16]], and less flap means less to clean up.

questions.q: At 250 feet the Bonanza rolls past the hold line onto runway 26 and stops. The learner keeps descending and looks at you. What do you do and say?
questions.a: Say 'Go around' in plain words [[25:99|AIH 4-6]]. A hazard on the runway is a listed reason [[24:181|AFH 9-10]], and an early go-around is in order when traffic may not clear [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]. The look at you is landing expectancy or indecision to debrief later [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

questions.q: The learner adds full power. The nose rises sharply and yaws left, and the stall horn chirps. What are you watching for, and what do you do?
questions.a: The elevator trim stall setup: propwash and nose-up trim pitching above climb attitude [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. Coach forward pressure, right rudder and rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; if the learner does not respond at once, take control without hesitation [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

questions.q: Climbing through 100 feet the learner reaches for the flap lever and pulls it all the way up while still holding heavy forward pressure. What can happen, and what should they have done?
questions.a: A sudden full retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and reaching for the handle under high control pressures risks control [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Flaps come up in small steps after the descent stops, as the airplane accelerates [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

questions.q: The Bonanza now starts its takeoff roll below you, and the Cessna on final calls a go-around too. Where do you fly, and what do you say?
questions.a: Offset slightly to the side to keep the Bonanza in sight [[24:272|AFH 13-23]], continue past the departure end before any turn [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]], and announce your position and intentions on the CTAF [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]. Back on downwind, redo the before-landing checklist [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. Then consider ending the day: fatigue is a human factor in your situational awareness [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on the approach and, after the go-around, review the balked-landing items and redo the before-landing checklist before the next approach, explaining why.
skills.practice: On every practice go-around, say 'Before-landing checklist again' on downwind and do it fully [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

skills.do: Make the right calls: tell the tower or CTAF you are going around and your intentions, and explain the towered 'go around' default.
skills.practice: Script both versions: towered (overfly, climb to pattern altitude, crosswind entry [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]) and nontowered (position report [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]]).

skills.do: Make a timely decision to discontinue the approach and say why, naming the gate or hazard that triggered it.
skills.practice: Fly approaches with a friend calling random 'hazards'; answer each with the decision and the reason within one breath [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

skills.do: Apply takeoff power immediately and transition to climb pitch attitude for VX or VY as appropriate ±5 knots (ACS AI.VII.N.S4), while explaining power, attitude and trim forces.
skills.practice: Trimmed full-flap glides at altitude, then full power: hold the climb picture against the trim and rough trim, saying each step [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Configure after a positive rate of climb is verified or as the manufacturer says: flaps in steps, gear after a positive rate and rough trim.
skills.practice: Call 'Descent stopped, flaps to takeoff' and 'Positive rate, gear up' out loud before moving each lever [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Side-step slightly to keep conflicting traffic in sight when needed, with a small coordinated turn, and explain the choice.
skills.practice: On go-arounds for simulated runway traffic, offset to the side, then fly parallel on the upwind leg [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

skills.do: Maintain VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude (ACS AI.VII.N.S7) while talking.
skills.practice: Fly go-arounds with nonstop patter; check the airspeed window at every 100 feet until it stays in.

skills.do: Keep directional control and the right wind-drift correction through the climb, changing from wing-low to a crab.
skills.practice: On crosswind days, go around from wing-low finals and narrate the change to a crab [[24:140|AFH 6-8]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common go-around errors, usually a simulated error the examiner flies as your learner.
skills.practice: For each AFH error, practice saying what you see, the cause and the fix in one breath [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

quiz.q: Which climb tolerance does the CFI ACS apply to you after a go-around while climbing at VY to a safe maneuvering altitude?
options: VY ±5 knots
VY +10/-5 knots
VY ±10 knots
VY +5/-0 knots
quiz.why: ACS AI.VII.N.S7: “Maintain VY ±5 knots to a safe maneuvering altitude.” The private standard is +10/-5 (ACS PA.IV.N.S7).

quiz.q: Per the AFH, full go-around power is held until what has been restored?
options: Pattern altitude and a steady VY climb
A positive rate on the VSI
Flying speed and controllability
Normal oil pressure and rpm
quiz.why: Apply full or maximum allowable power smoothly and hold it until flying speed and controllability are restored [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: At what point does the AFH have the landing flaps first come partly up?
options: As soon as full power is applied
After the descent has stopped
Only after reaching VY
After the landing gear is up
quiz.why: After the descent has been stopped, the landing flaps are partially retracted or set to takeoff as the manufacturer recommends [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH call it good practice to extend the same flaps at the same point in the pattern on every landing?
options: It keeps the flap motor within its duty cycle
It gives a preplanned, familiar go-around sequence
It keeps the stall speed equal on every leg
It is a standard item in most POH procedures
quiz.why: Consistent flap use allows a preplanned and familiar go-around sequence based on the airplane's position in the pattern [[24:236|AFH 12-5]].

quiz.q: When an approach is going badly, which instruction does the AIH say works better than an abstract one?
options: 'Take appropriate measures'
'Go around'
'Fix your energy state'
'Do what you think is best'
quiz.why: Telling a learner to take appropriate measures might not get the desired action; telling them to conduct a go-around has one shared meaning [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

quiz.q: AC 91-79B says the pilot is responsible for telling ATC when an instruction will produce what?
options: A landing beyond the touchdown zone
A tailwind component of more than 10 knots on short final
An unstabilized approach due to speed or descent rate
A touchdown at more than VREF plus 10 knots
quiz.why: It is the pilot's responsibility to inform ATC when compliance with an instruction will result in an unstabilized approach due to speed or descent rate [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.1]].

quiz.q: What minimum weather does the AIM say should exist before a pilot receives a LAHSO clearance?
options: A 500-foot ceiling and 1 mile visibility
A 1,000-foot ceiling and 3 miles visibility
A 1,500-foot ceiling and 5 statute miles visibility
A 3,000-foot ceiling and 5 miles visibility
quiz.why: Pilots should only receive a LAHSO clearance with a minimum ceiling of 1,000 feet and 3 statute miles visibility [[33:256|AIM 4-3-11]].

quiz.q: A rapid acceleration with poor visual references can produce the somatogravic illusion. What does the pilot feel, and what may they do?
options: A nose-low feel, so they pull toward a stall
A nose-up feel, so they push into a dive
A left bank, so they roll to the right
A climb, so they reduce power to idle
quiz.why: Rapid acceleration creates the illusion of a nose-up attitude, and the disoriented pilot may push into a nose-low or dive attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]].

quiz.q: Per AC 90-66C, what should an airplane executing a go-around at a nontowered airport do first?
options: Turn crosswind once it reaches 400 feet AGL
Make a 45-degree turn away from the pattern
Continue straight ahead past the departure end
Turn right away toward the upwind side of the field
quiz.why: Airplanes executing a go-around should continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end of the runway, aware of pattern traffic [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]].

quiz.q: Why does the AFH want the landing gear left down until the airplane is sure to stay airborne?
options: It may touch down early in a low go-around
Raising the gear raises the stall speed sharply
The gear motor robs the engine of full power
Gear retraction causes a strong nose-down pitch
quiz.why: If the airplane touches down as the go-around starts, the gear should be down and locked; retract it after a positive rate and rough trim, when it will surely stay airborne [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Short final at 150 feet: your learner is 7 knots slow, a bit low, and the stall horn chirps in a gust. They say, 'I'll add a little power and land.' What is the best instructor call?
options: Let them continue and add power; a chirp in a gust is normal on short final
'Go around': full power, hold a safe attitude, let it accelerate before climbing
Have them raise the flaps one notch to reduce drag and stretch the glide
Take the controls, pull up firmly and climb at VX to get away from the ground
final_quiz.why: An airplane cannot climb below minimum power required speed, so resist pitching up when slow; sometimes lower the nose briefly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Retracting flaps on an undershoot adds risk [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

final_quiz.q: At altitude you demonstrate an elevator trim stall. With full power in, the nose rises past the climb attitude and the stall warning sounds. What comes next?
options: Close the throttle so that the nose drops and the stall warning stops
Raise all the flaps at once to remove the pitch-up
Let it fully stall so the learner sees how deep it goes
Push forward to kill the warning, set climb attitude, then trim
final_quiz.why: Apply enough forward pressure to reduce angle of attack and eliminate the warning, return to the normal climb attitude, then trim to relieve the heavy pressures [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your commercial applicant in a retractable single wants to raise the gear the moment power is in, 'because it's the biggest drag.' What do you teach?
options: Agree: on most airplanes the gear is the largest drag item
Flaps partly first, then gear after a positive rate and rough trim
Leave both down until reaching pattern altitude
Raise the gear and flaps together to save time
final_quiz.why: Unless the AFM/POH says otherwise, flaps come up at least partly first: full flaps usually make more drag, and the gear should be down if the airplane touches. Gear comes up after a positive rate, rough trim and certainty of staying airborne [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

final_quiz.q: Lesson at a 6,000-foot field on a hot day. Your learner's sea-level habit is a firm pull to the usual climb picture. What do you brief?
options: The same picture will give the same climb
Expect a lower climb pitch and a weaker climb
Use VX for the whole go-around climb
Use the same pitch with half the flaps
final_quiz.why: Climb pitch will be lower when power is limited by density altitude [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]; thin air cuts power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

final_quiz.q: Gusty afternoon, towering cumulus nearby. On short final the airspeed suddenly jumps 15 knots. Your learner smiles and says 'free energy.' What do you teach?
options: Use it to land shorter by pulling the power
A large gain near convection may come before a loss: go around
Lower the nose to hold the target approach speed and continue to land
Hold the speed gain all the way into the flare
final_quiz.why: A rapid airspeed increase near convective weather may be a sign of a coming decrease and a reason to discontinue the approach [[28:273|AWH 22-18]].

final_quiz.q: You accepted 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 33.' At 20 feet you balloon badly and go around while a Cessna is departing on 33. What is right?
options: You may not go around once you have accepted the hold-short
Climb straight ahead over the intersection and call the tower after landing
Keep the Cessna in sight, stay clear of it, and promptly tell the tower
Land anyway and use maximum braking to stop short of 33
final_quiz.why: LAHSO does not preclude a rejected landing; maintain safe separation from other aircraft and promptly notify the controller [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. Offsetting to keep traffic in sight is the AFH technique [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

final_quiz.q: In a high-performance single, full power produces heavy forward pressure. Your learner lets go with the right hand to reach for the flap lever and the nose climbs. What does the AFH say?
options: Reach for flaps first, since drag is the bigger risk
Use caution reaching for flaps; control comes first
Use both hands on the yoke until reaching VY
Retract the gear before touching the flaps
final_quiz.why: In airplanes with high control pressures at maximum power, use caution reaching for the flap handle; airplane control is the first consideration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: After two go-arounds your learner says, 'Sorry, I keep blowing these approaches.' Which response fits the sources best?
options: 'You're right; we'll keep drilling approaches until you never need go-arounds again.'
'Those were good calls. Any approach can end in a go-around; tell me what you saw.'
'Don't worry about it; just try to land the next one no matter what.'
'Let's skip go-arounds today and work only on landings instead.'
final_quiz.why: The idea that a go-around always means a poor approach or lack of skill is a fallacy [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], and satisfying outcomes strengthen behavior [[25:63|AIH 3-12]].

final_quiz.q: Night go-around over a dark area off the runway end. At full power your learner says 'we're pitching up too much' and pushes the nose down, though the attitude indicator shows a normal climb. What is happening?
options: An elevator trim stall is developing
The somatogravic illusion from the acceleration
Ground effect is ending, so the nose drops on its own
A tailwind shear is lowering the nose
final_quiz.why: Rapid acceleration with poor visual references creates a false nose-up feeling, and the pilot may push into a nose-low attitude [[23:73|IFH 3-6]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

final_quiz.q: You go around because a slower airplane is still rolling out on the runway. Why does the AFH suggest a slight offset rather than staying over the centerline?
options: To keep the conflicting traffic in sight
To shorten the pattern for a faster return
To stay out of your own propwash
To avoid ground effect off the runway
final_quiz.why: If the go-around is due to conflicting traffic, consider maneuvering to the side to keep it in sight, which may mean a slight turn to offset [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner says 'Go around,' then sets about half power to 'ease into it' and holds it. What does the AFH call for?
options: Half power is fine if the airplane is not sinking
Full power smoothly and without hesitation
Abrupt full power to stop the descent quickly
Half power until the flaps are fully retracted
final_quiz.why: The instant the decision is made, full or maximum allowable power is applied smoothly, without hesitation; abrupt movements can make some engines falter [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: The POH landing distance assumes touchdown within a set air distance. Your learner floats far past the aiming point on a short runway. Per AC 91-79B, why is that a go-around cue?
options: Brakes overheat after a long float
The calculated landing distance may not be achievable
The tower must cancel the landing clearance at that point
A long float always ends in a bounce
final_quiz.why: If the airplane does not touch down within the air distance included in the AFM/POH landing distance, it may not be possible to achieve the calculated landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.4]].

final_quiz.q: After a go-around from a wing-low final, your learner holds the bank and opposite rudder up to 800 feet. What do you teach?
options: Correct: hold the sideslip all the way to pattern altitude
Once climbing, turn into the wind, level the wings and crab
Level the wings and center the rudder, letting it drift
Increase the bank to hold the centerline more tightly
final_quiz.why: As the climb is established, turn the nose into the wind, level the wings and adjust rudder to crab, checking the ground track often [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

takeaways: You hold VX or VY ±5 knots while explaining; your private learner is held to +10/-5 (ACS AI.VII.N.S4, S7).
Power, attitude, configuration, in that order [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Expect strong nose-up and left-yaw forces from landing trim: forward pressure, right rudder, rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Flaps come up in steps after the descent stops; the gear after a positive rate and rough trim [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
Delay comes from landing expectancy and pride; teach from day one that any approach may end in a go-around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].
Use the plain words 'Go around' and let learners make the call themselves [[25:99|AIH 4-6]] [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
After the go-around, redo the full before-landing checklist [[24:272|AFH 13-23]].
cfi_notes: If no crosswind exists on test day, expect the examiner to test the wind-drift elements orally. Have the wing-low to crab patter ready [[24:140|AFH 6-8]].

Sources differ on airspeed windows: the AFH stabilized criteria allow +10/-5 KIAS of the recommended landing speed on the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]], but your go-around climb standard is ±5 knots of VX or VY (ACS AI.VII.N.S4 and S7). Do not mix them up when briefing.

Several key lines (maneuver to the side for traffic, level flight while accelerating from a low-speed go-around, redo the before-landing checklist, flaps before gear) are printed in the AFH twin-engine chapter [[24:272|AFH 13-23]]. The single-engine section says the same about flaps and gear [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]; the rest is general good practice, so present it as such.

Pattern guidance after a go-around differs slightly by source: AC 90-66C and the PHAK say continue straight ahead until beyond the departure end [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.6]] [[1:355|PHAK 14-21]]; the AFH describes an upwind leg with a shallow turn to the upwind side at a safe altitude [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]; at a tower, the P/CG default is overfly the runway and enter crosswind [[34:353|AIM P/CG]]. Teach the nontowered rule and the towered default separately.

The AIM low-approach paragraph says to fly straight ahead with no turns until a visual check for traffic, unless ATC authorizes otherwise [[33:256|AIM 4-3-12]]. That is not in conflict with a small offset to keep traffic in sight; it is the reason to keep the offset slight.
The somatogravic illusion is described for takeoff acceleration [[23:73|IFH 3-6]]; applying it to a night go-around is reasoning, not a quoted source. Say so if asked.

The elevator trim stall is a demonstration-only maneuver that only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform on a practical test [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. It is the best ground-to-air bridge for this Task; brief it on the ground first.
The AFH uses 'student' and the AIH uses 'learner.' Same person.
gaps: Go-around flap settings, the order of flap and gear retraction, carburetor heat and mixture handling, and gear retraction speeds are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.

No source defines 'safe maneuvering altitude' for the ACS. The AFH keeps takeoff power to at least 500 feet above terrain on a normal departure [[24:137|AFH 6-5]]; brief your own number with the learner and the examiner.
No source gives a mixture procedure for a go-around at a high-elevation airport; the PHAK only explains why full rich can cost power there [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].
No source gives a method for instructor-called versus learner-called go-arounds or how often to practice them; the teaching table here is application of the AIH principles.
Available Landing Distance for LAHSO is in the Chart Supplement and Terminal Procedures Publications, which are not in the resources [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

activities.title: Gates, margins and go-around triggers
activities.intro: Work each one from the lesson's rules, then type your answer.

items.q: IFR practice approach to a field at 1,430 feet MSL in instrument conditions. By what altimeter reading must the approach be stabilized, or you go around?
items.why: The IMC gate is 1,000 feet above airport elevation [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]: 1,430 + 1,000 = 2,430 feet MSL.

items.q: POH landing distance over a 50-foot obstacle is 1,900 feet; the runway is 2,600 feet. Using the AC 91-79B rule, what threshold crossing height uses up the whole 700-foot margin?
items.why: Each 10 feet above 50 adds about 200 feet [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]. 700 / 200 = 3.5 steps; 3.5 x 10 = 35 feet; 50 + 35 = 85 feet.

items.q: Your learner's approach speed is 65 knots and the POH landing distance is 1,500 feet. They cross the threshold at 71.5 knots, 10% fast. About what landing distance now?
items.why: 71.5 / 65 = 1.10, a 10% increase, which costs about 20% more distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.2]]: 1,500 x 1.20 = 1,800 feet.

items.q: A Cessna 150 chart note says to increase distances by 10% for each 2 knots of tailwind. POH landing distance 1,200 feet, 4-knot tailwind. About what distance?
Nontowered field, elevation 650 feet, pattern altitude 1,000 feet AGL. After a go-around, what is the lowest altitude at which you may begin the crosswind turn (beyond the departure end)?
items.why: Pattern altitude is 650 + 1,000 = 1,650 feet MSL; turn within 300 feet of it [[17:15|AC 90-66C 11.7]]: 1,650 - 300 = 1,350 feet MSL.

items.q: POH: VX 60 KIAS, VY 72 KIAS. You go around toward trees and choose VX. What is the highest airspeed that still meets your CFI standard?

activities.title: Elevator trim stall demonstration, step by step
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the AFH demonstration steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: At a safe altitude, clear the area of other traffic
Slowly retard the throttle and extend the gear, if retractable
Extend flaps to half or full, close the throttle and hold altitude to glide speed
Establish the glide and trim nose-up for the normal approach
Advance the throttle smoothly to maximum allowable power, as for a go-around
As the nose rises and turns left toward a stall, apply forward pressure to kill the warning
Return to the normal climb attitude and adjust trim to relieve the pressures
Complete the normal go-around procedures and return to the desired flightpath

activities.title: Power, attitude or configuration?
activities.intro: Tap each action, then tap the AFH go-around principle it falls under.

items.t: Advance to maximum allowable power smoothly, without hesitation
Hold considerable forward elevator pressure against landing trim
Lower the nose briefly to gain airspeed when slow
Rough trim once airspeed and climb pitch are set
Right rudder for torque and P-factor
Landing flaps partly up after the descent stops
Gear up after a positive rate of climb

activities.title: True or false: what the AFH really says
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH lists indecision and delay in initiating a go-around as two separate common errors.
cards.why: True. Both appear on the list of ten common go-around errors [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

cards.s: When a go-around starts from very low airspeed, pitch straight to the VY attitude so the climb begins at once.
cards.why: False. Temper the pitch-up; a few moments of level or near-level flight may be needed while the airplane accelerates [[24:272|AFH 13-23]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: The AFH says the go-around maneuver is dangerous in itself, so it should be avoided whenever possible.
cards.why: False. It is not inherently dangerous; it becomes dangerous only when delayed unduly or done improperly [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

cards.s: Raising the flaps is a good way to fix an undershoot on final because it cuts drag.
cards.why: False. It can cause a sudden loss of lift, an excessive sink rate and a worse unstable approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

cards.s: With full flaps and nose-up trim, the pitch-up from go-around power does not fully disappear when the flaps are raised.
cards.why: True. The trim setting keeps some of it, so expect rapid changes in pitch forces [[24:235|AFH 12-4]].

cards.s: Ground effect gives a real cushion of air that makes an early climb safe at full power.
cards.why: False. The cushion is imaginary; reduced induced drag is borrowed performance repaid on climbing out [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

activities.title: The pattern after a go-around
activities.intro: Drag each rule to the numbered point on the pattern where it applies.

pins.label: After a go-around, keep straight ahead past here
Turn here only within 300 ft of pattern altitude
Finish this turn at least 1/4 mile out
Hold pattern altitude until abeam the approach end
Enter level, at pattern altitude, abeam midfield

activities.title: Hazard and defense
activities.intro: Match each go-around hazard with the defense the sources give.

pairs.l: A rejected landing after accepting LAHSO
pairs.r: Keep safe separation and promptly notify the controller

pairs.l: A vehicle or aircraft entering your runway on final
pairs.r: Go around early and inform the controller

pairs.l: A larger aircraft departing ahead as you climb out
pairs.r: Stay above its climb path; avoid headings below and behind it

pairs.l: The turn to final would create a collision hazard
pairs.r: Go around or make an avoidance maneuver

pairs.l: A false nose-up feeling at full power over a dark area
pairs.r: Trust the attitude indicator over the inner ear

pairs.l: Heavy pitch forces while reaching for the flap lever
pairs.r: Fly the airplane first; configure once control is solid

activities.title: Teaching the first go-arounds
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner has about 12 hours and has flown only full-stop landings with you calling any go-arounds. Today's lesson is go-arounds. It unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On the ground, the learner says, 'I hope I never need one of these.' What is the best opening for the brief?
options: 'Good pilots rarely need them, so focus on good approaches.'
'Any approach can end in a go-around; it is a normal maneuver we will practice.'
'We will only do one today so it does not become a habit.'
'Let's skip the brief and learn it by feel in the air.'
steps.why: Emphasize early that any approach may end in a go-around; the failure idea is a fallacy [[24:181|AFH 9-10]] [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

steps.s: Before any pattern work, where do you first let the learner feel the go-around trim forces?
options: On short final, with no warning
At a safe altitude, with a trimmed glide and full power
During a touch-and-go on the runway
In the run-up area, with power and full flaps
steps.why: The elevator trim stall demonstration is done at a safe altitude after clearing the area [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

steps.s: First pattern go-around. At 200 feet you want it now. What do you say?
options: 'Maybe consider going around.'
'Go around.'
'Take appropriate action.'
'Watch your approach, it is getting bad.'
steps.why: Concrete words get the desired action; 'go around' has one shared meaning [[25:99|AIH 4-6]].

steps.s: Power comes in, the nose pitches up hard, the learner freezes and the stall horn starts. What do you do?
options: Wait and see if the learner recovers alone
Take control without hesitation, then hand it back
Tell them to raise the flaps to stop the pitch
Reduce the power to idle to lower the nose
steps.why: On hazardous maneuvers be ready to take control, and do not hesitate when the learner needs it [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

steps.s: Later circuits go well when you call them. How do you test whether the learner can recognize the need alone?
options: Call every go-around for the rest of training
Let a mild error develop, safety permitting, and see if they call it
Ask them to recite the AFH error list in flight
Have them land every approach, good or bad
steps.why: Safety permitting, let learners go partway into a mistake and find the way out; vary the maneuver to test understanding [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].
